cls: Systemic/urinary alkalinizing agent; antacid; anticoagulant (in vitro / blood products)
quick: 10-30 mL of sodium citrate solution diluted in water, 3-4 times daily after meals
Take after meals diluted in water to reduce GI upset
Used (e.g., 0.3 M sodium citrate for aspiration prophylaxis) - generally acceptable
Avoid/caution in renal impairment - sodium and alkali load, hyperkalemia risk
Caution in severe hepatic impairment (impaired citrate metabolism)
Serum electrolytes, bicarbonate, urine pH, sodium
summary: Sodium citrate is an alkalinizing salt that is metabolized to bicarbonate, raising blood and urine pH. It is used to alkalinize urine (e.g., to relieve dysuria, prevent uric-acid/cystine stones, and aid excretion of certain drugs), to treat or prevent metabolic acidosis, as a fast-acting non-particulate antacid for aspiration prophylaxis before anesthesia (e.g., obstetric), and as an in-vitro/extracorporeal anticoagulant for stored blood and citrate dialysis/apheresis. Its main cautions are sodium load and use in renal impairment.
indications: Alkalinization of urine (relief of dysuria/cystitis discomfort; prevention of uric-acid and cystine renal stones)
Treatment and prevention of chronic metabolic acidosis (e.g., renal tubular acidosis)
Non-particulate antacid for prophylaxis against acid aspiration before general anesthesia or obstetric anesthesia
Anticoagulation of stored blood/blood components and in regional citrate anticoagulation for apheresis/dialysis (extracorporeal)

dosage.d: Sodium citrate sachet/solution providing ~4 g, 3 times daily for up to 48 h
dosage.n: Dissolve in water; short-term symptomatic use

dosage.d: 10-30 mL diluted in water, 3-4 times daily after meals
dosage.n: Titrate to target urine pH; take after meals

dosage.d: 5-15 mL diluted in water, 3-4 times daily after meals
dosage.n: Titrate to effect and urine pH

dosage.d: 30 mL of 0.3 M sodium citrate orally
dosage.n: Given shortly before induction of anesthesia

admin: Dilute oral solution/sachets in water and take after meals to minimize gastric irritation and the laxative/saline effect
For aspiration prophylaxis give the 0.3 M solution shortly before anesthesia
Maintain adequate fluid intake during urinary alkalinization
Extracorporeal/blood-bank citrate is handled per transfusion/apheresis protocol, not ingested
moa: Citrate ion is metabolized in the liver (via the tricarboxylic acid cycle) to bicarbonate, which raises plasma and urinary pH (systemic and urinary alkalinization). In stored blood and extracorporeal circuits, citrate chelates ionized calcium, blocking the calcium-dependent coagulation cascade and preventing clotting.

absolute: Hypocalcemia or conditions requiring calcium (for the anticoagulant chelating effect)
Severe sodium-restricted states (e.g., decompensated heart failure)
monitor: Serum sodium, potassium, calcium, and bicarbonate

preg: Oral sodium citrate, including 0.3 M solution for aspiration prophylaxis in obstetric anesthesia, is widely used and generally considered acceptable. Use the lowest effective dose and account for sodium load.
lact: Considered compatible with breastfeeding. Citrate and resulting bicarbonate are normal body constituents.
renal: Use with great caution; avoid in significant renal impairment. Reduced renal function impairs excretion of the sodium and alkali load and raises the risk of hyperkalemia, metabolic alkalosis, and fluid overload.
hepatic: Use cautiously in severe hepatic impairment, where conversion of citrate to bicarbonate is reduced, potentially causing citrate accumulation and hypocalcemia (especially with large extracorporeal citrate loads).

major: Potassium-sparing diuretics, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, potassium supplements (additive hyperkalemia)
moderate: Aluminium-containing antacids (urinary alkalinization increases aluminium absorption)
Drugs whose excretion is pH-dependent (e.g., quinidine, salicylates, methenamine, lithium - altered clearance)
Calcium-containing products (counteract citrate anticoagulant effect; risk of stones with milk-alkali)
minor: Iron salts (reduced absorption in alkaline urine/gut)
interactions.food: Take after meals diluted in water; milk-alkali risk with excessive calcium intake
interactions.diagnostics: Raises serum bicarbonate and urine pH; large extracorporeal citrate loads can lower ionized calcium

serious: Hyperkalemia (especially with renal impairment or potassium-sparing drugs)
Hypocalcemia / tetany (large citrate loads, extracorporeal use)
emergency: Symptomatic hypocalcemia with tetany or arrhythmia

monitoring: Ionized calcium during extracorporeal/regional citrate anticoagulation
Signs of fluid overload, especially in cardiac/renal disease
counsel: Dissolve the powder/solution in water and take after food
Drink plenty of fluids when using it to alkalinize urine
Tell your doctor if you have kidney, heart, or blood-pressure problems
Do not use long term without medical advice
Stop and seek help if you get tingling, muscle cramps, confusion, or marked swelling
pk: Antacid effect almost immediate; urinary alkalinization within hours
Rise in plasma bicarbonate within ~1-2 hours of an oral dose
Citrate is rapidly metabolized to bicarbonate; not described as a fixed plasma half-life
Short - several hours; requires repeated dosing for sustained alkalinization
Store at room temperature 15-30 C; keep solutions tightly closed; protect from freezing
pearls: Citrate becomes bicarbonate after hepatic metabolism - effectively a 'pro-bicarbonate' alkalinizer
Excellent non-particulate antacid for aspiration prophylaxis (e.g., 30 mL of 0.3 M before obstetric anesthesia)
Same chelating chemistry makes it the standard anticoagulant for stored blood and regional citrate dialysis/apheresis - watch ionized calcium
Significant sodium load - caution in heart failure, hypertension, and renal impairment (regional/EMA-BNF product information, not a single FDA monograph)
missed: For scheduled oral alkalinizing therapy, take the missed dose when remembered unless it is nearly time for the next dose, then skip it. Do not double up. Single pre-anesthetic aspiration-prophylaxis doses are not 'missed' - they are given once before surgery.
overdose: Excess intake causes metabolic alkalosis, hypernatremia, hypokalemia or hyperkalemia, fluid overload, and (with large citrate loads) hypocalcemia and tetany. Stop the drug and provide supportive care: correct electrolytes and acid-base disturbance, give calcium for symptomatic hypocalcemia, and manage fluid status.
